title: Package clause
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Declares a module named orders
Names the package this file belongs to
Imports a package named orders
explanation: Every .go file begins with a package clause; all files in a directory share one package, and there is no mod-style file tree.

title: Import
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Brings two standard packages into scope
Re-exports fmt and strings to callers
Declares two modules in this directory
explanation: Imports are by path and used through the package name; an unused import is a compile error, not a warning.

title: Short variable declaration
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Assigns to an existing variable
Declares a new variable
Compares the two sides for equality
explanation: Like let, but variables are mutable by default and there is no mut; := only works inside functions.

title: var declaration
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Declares an immutable total
Declares total, initialized to 0
Declares total, must be assigned before use
explanation: Go has no uninitialized variables: every type has a zero value, 0 for numbers, "" for strings, nil for pointers.

title: Multiple assignment
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Swaps the two values in one statement
Assigns b to both variables
Declares a tuple
explanation: The right side is evaluated fully before any assignment, so this is a swap without a temporary, like a destructuring assignment.

title: Constant
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A package-level variable, changeable at runtime
A constant visible only inside the function below
A compile-time constant with no written type
explanation: Constants may omit the type; an untyped constant takes whatever type the use site needs.

title: iota
code:
type Level int

const (
	Debug Level = iota
	Info
	Warn
	Error
)
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A random starting value
The length of the const block
A counter: 0, 1, 2, 3 down the block
explanation: iota restarts at 0 in each const block and increments per line; later lines repeat the previous expression, which is how Go spells an enum.

title: Blank identifier
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A placeholder assigned later
A variable named underscore
Discards that result
explanation: Same as _ in Rust; Go refuses unused local variables, so unwanted results must go to _.

title: Type declaration
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An alias; UserID and string are interchangeable
A string constant named UserID
A new distinct type whose underlying type is string
explanation: A defined type is distinct: passing a plain string where a UserID is expected does not compile, like a newtype in Rust.

title: Type alias
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Another name for the same type
A new type distinct from the function type
A variable that holds a function
explanation: With = it is an alias, not a new type: any func(Request) Response is a Handler and vice versa.

title: Case and visibility
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An exported field, visible outside the package
An optional field
A private field, invisible outside the package
explanation: There is no pub: an uppercase first letter means exported, lowercase means package-private, for fields, functions and types alike.

title: Package-level variable
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A compile-time constant of the package
A mutable variable shared by the package
A variable local to the newClient function
explanation: Package-level vars are initialized before main runs and are mutable; := is not allowed at package level, only var.

title: Sized integers
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A signed 8-bit integer
An 8-element array
An unsigned 8-bit integer
explanation: Go has int8 to int64, uint8 to uint64 and the platform-sized int and uint; byte is another name for uint8.

title: int
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An arbitrary-precision integer
An integer that is always 32 bits wide
The platform-sized signed integer
explanation: int is 64 bits on 64-bit platforms and is what len, cap and loop counters use, like isize but used everywhere.

title: Floating point
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Converts the int length to float64
Rounds the length to a whole number
Checks that the length fits in a float
explanation: Go never converts numeric types implicitly, so an int must be converted explicitly before it can divide a float64.

title: Strings are immutable
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Fails: strings cannot change
Appends into msg's existing memory
Builds a new string and rebinds msg to it
explanation: Strings are immutable values; += allocates a new one, like String in Rust being replaced rather than pushed into.

title: Raw string literal
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A raw string, backslashes kept as written
A comment spanning a single line
A compiled regular expression value
explanation: Backquoted strings have no escapes and may span lines, like r"..." in Rust; double-quoted ones interpret \n and friends.

title: Indexing a string
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: The first byte, not the first character
The first whitespace-separated word
The first Unicode character of s
explanation: Indexing a string gives bytes; a non-ASCII character spans several bytes, so use range or []rune for characters.

title: Runes
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Iterates the raw bytes of the string
Iterates whitespace-separated words
Iterates Unicode characters
explanation: range over a string yields runes (Unicode code points, like char), while s[i] yields bytes.

title: Explicit conversion
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Casts away the sign
Calls a function named float64
Converts the int to a float64
explanation: T(x) is Go's only conversion syntax, used for numbers, strings and bytes alike; there is no as keyword.

title: Untyped constant
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Multiplies two plain integers
The constant becomes a Duration here
Does not compile: int times Duration
explanation: An untyped constant takes the type its context needs, so 5 can be an int, a float64 or a time.Duration depending on use.

title: Booleans
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Assigns Paid to Shipped
True when paid and not yet shipped
Bitwise and of two flags
explanation: Booleans are their own type; ints do not convert to bool, so there is no if n { } shortcut.

title: String formatting
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Builds and returns a string
Prints a line to standard output
Writes a line to the log file
explanation: Sprintf returns the string and Printf prints it; %s is a string, %d an integer, %v anything.

title: Function parameters
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: One int parameter; a has no type
Two parameters, both int
One tuple parameter
explanation: Types come after names, and adjacent parameters of the same type share one type; the result type follows the parentheses.

title: Multiple results
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Returns either an int or an error
One tuple result
Two results: the value and an error
explanation: Not a Result and not a tuple, just two return values; by convention the error is last and nil on success.

title: Named results
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Returns nothing
Returns zero values
Returns the current n and err
explanation: Named results are variables; a bare return sends back whatever they hold, which deferred functions can still modify.

title: Variadic parameter
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Any number of ints, seen as a slice
Exactly three int arguments
A pointer to a single int value
explanation: A variadic parameter is a []int inside the function; call it as sum(1, 2, 3) or sum(xs...) to spread a slice.

title: Spreading a slice
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Passes each element as a separate argument
Copies the slice
Passes the slice as one argument
explanation: The trailing ... unpacks a slice into a variadic call, where the bare slice would be one argument.

title: Function value
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A generic type parameter named f
A parameter holding a function
A method named f on the int type
explanation: Function types are written inline, func(int) int, with no Fn/FnMut/FnOnce distinction; functions are ordinary values.

title: Closure
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A function returning a copy of n
A method defined on int
An anonymous function sharing n
explanation: Closures capture variables, not values, so each call to the returned function increments the same n; no move or borrow annotations.

title: defer
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Unlocks immediately
Unlocks when the function returns
Unlocks on a background thread
explanation: There is no Drop; cleanup is done with defer, which runs when the enclosing function returns, last in first out.

title: defer order
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Runs after the body, before the first one
Runs after the first deferred call
Runs immediately when reached
explanation: Deferred calls run in reverse order of registration, like a stack of destructors.

title: panic
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Aborts the program with that message
Logs a warning and continues
Returns an error to the caller
explanation: panic is for unrecoverable bugs and runs deferred functions on the way out; expected failures use error values instead.

title: recover
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Resets err back to nil
Catches a panic in progress
Retries f until it succeeds
explanation: recover only works inside a deferred function and turns a panic into a value, roughly catch_unwind.

title: init
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Runs automatically when the package loads
A constructor called by the user
The entry point of the program
explanation: Each file may have init functions that run once before main, after package variables are initialized; nothing calls them explicitly.

title: Method value
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A pointer to the Counter c
A function with c already bound as receiver
A copy of the method's source code
explanation: c.Inc without parentheses is a method value with the receiver already bound, like a bound method in Python.

title: if with a statement
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Declares two package-level variables
Looks up first, then uses ok as the condition
Two separate conditions, both must hold
explanation: An if may start with one statement; the condition follows the semicolon, and v is scoped to the if.

title: else
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A second condition tried if the first fails
A loop that keeps running while n is zero
A match arm guarded by a condition
explanation: else and else if must sit on the same line as the closing brace; braces are mandatory and conditions take no parentheses.

title: Three-clause for
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A loop over a range object
An infinite loop
A counted loop from 0 to len-1
explanation: for is the only loop keyword; this C-style form is used when you need the index arithmetic, otherwise range is preferred.

title: for as while
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Loops over the queue's elements
Loops while the condition holds
Loops exactly once
explanation: A for with just a condition is Go's while; there is no while keyword.

title: Infinite for
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Loops until return, break or panic
A block that runs exactly once
Runs the block exactly zero times
explanation: for with no clauses is loop {} in Rust; the usual exit is return or break.

title: range over a slice
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Iterates: i is the index, item the element
Iterates the keys and values of a map
Iterates: i is the element, item the index
explanation: range yields the index and a copy of the element; to skip the index write for _, item := range items.

title: range over a map
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Iterates the values, ignoring keys
Iterates the keys, ignoring values
Iterates index and value pairs
explanation: range over a map yields key and value in no fixed order; iteration order is deliberately randomized.

title: range over an int
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Loops three times
Loops over the digits of 3
Loops until f returns 3
explanation: Since Go 1.22 range over an integer n runs n times, like for _ in 0..3.

title: switch
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Matches a two-element tuple
Runs two cases one after another
Matches either value
explanation: A case may list several values, like "paused" | "stopped"; every case breaks automatically, nothing falls through.

title: switch without a value
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Switches on an empty struct value
Loops over every case in order
Picks the first case that is true
explanation: A switch with no expression is an if-else chain that reads top to bottom; the first true case wins.

title: fallthrough
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Continues into the next case body
Jumps straight to the default case
Exits the switch immediately
explanation: Cases never fall through by default; the fallthrough keyword asks for it explicitly, and it is rare.

title: Labeled break
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Exits both loops at once
Jumps back to the start of the outer loop
Exits only the inner loop
explanation: Labels let break and continue target an outer loop, like 'outer: in Rust.

title: continue
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Exits the loop
Skips to the next iteration
Restarts the loop from the beginning
explanation: continue and break work as in C and Rust.

title: Array
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A slice that can grow with append
A fixed-size array, copied by value
A pointer to four bytes
explanation: [N]T is a value type with the length in the type, like [u8; 4], and APIs use slices instead.

title: Slice literal
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A growable list with 4 elements
A set of 4 distinct values
A fixed-length array of 4
explanation: []T is a slice, the Vec<T> of Go; [4]int would be a fixed array.

title: make for slices
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A pointer to an int array
A slice of n zeros, ready to index
An empty slice with room for n
explanation: make([]T, len) allocates len zero elements; make([]T, 0, cap) is the empty-with-capacity form, like Vec::with_capacity.

title: len and cap
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: The number of elements in s
The size of the backing array
The largest element of s
explanation: len is the element count and cap the size of the backing array; append reallocates only when len reaches cap.

title: append
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Appends and keeps the returned slice
Builds a new array; the old slice is unchanged
Appends in place; the result can be dropped
explanation: append may reallocate, so it is always written s = append(s, x); dropping the result is a bug.

title: Appending a slice
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Appends b as a single nested element
Appends every element of b to a
Concatenates into a new array, a untouched
explanation: The ... spreads b into the variadic append, which may write into a's spare capacity, so the result is the new slice.

title: Slice expression
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: The element at index 3
A view of the first 3 elements
An independent copy of the first 3
explanation: Like &v[..3], a view that shares memory; modifying the result modifies items, and there is no borrow checker to warn you.

title: copy
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Copies elements from items into out
Appends items to out
Makes out an alias of items
explanation: copy(dst, src) copies min(len) elements between overlapping-safe slices; slices.Clone(items) is the one-liner.

title: nil slice
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A slice that must be made before use
A nil slice, usable with append and len
A pointer that will panic on append
explanation: The zero slice is nil, has length 0, and append works on it; there is no need to make it first.

title: Map literal
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A struct with two integer fields
A hash map with initial entries
An ordered list of string-int pairs
explanation: map[K]V is the built-in hash map, like HashMap<K, V>; literal entries are key: value.

title: make for maps
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Creates a fixed-size array
Declares the map type without allocating
Creates an empty, writable map
explanation: A map must be made before writing; a declared but un-made map is nil, readable but panics on write.

title: Map lookup
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Looks up id; panics if it is missing
Looks up id; ok says if it exists
Looks up two keys at the same time
explanation: Map lookup does not return an Option: a missing key yields the zero value, and the second result tells you whether it was there.

title: Map update
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Increments the count, from 0 if new
Panics because the key is missing
Appends v to the map's key list
explanation: Reading a missing key gives the zero value, so n[v]++ works without an entry check; no entry().or_insert dance.

title: delete
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Marks the session as deleted
Removes the key from the map
Frees the whole map
explanation: delete is a builtin; deleting a missing key is a no-op, not an error.

title: Set as a map
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A set: keys with zero-size values
A map with no values allowed
A map from string to an empty struct type name
explanation: Go has no set type; a map to the empty struct is the idiom, since struct{} takes no memory.

title: Sorting
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A function returning the sorted slice
A less-than function comparing two positions
A filter keeping younger users
explanation: sort.Slice sorts in place with a less(i, j) callback over indexes; slices.SortFunc takes a cmp(a, b) int instead.

title: Struct type
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An enum with two variants
A tuple type
A type with two named fields
explanation: Field types follow field names; there is no derive, and the type is comparable and copyable by default.

title: Struct literal
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Builds a map
Calls a function named User
Builds a User value by field name
explanation: Like a Rust struct literal but with colons; any field left out takes its zero value.

title: Zero-value struct
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An uninitialized Counter, unusable
A nil pointer to a Counter
A Counter with all fields zeroed
explanation: Every type has a usable zero value, so a struct declared with var is already valid; many types are designed to work without a constructor.

title: Taking an address
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A pointer to u
A reference counted handle
A copy of u
explanation: & takes an address and * dereferences, as in C, but there is no pointer arithmetic and no ownership rules.

title: Field through a pointer
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Does not compile; needs (*p).Name
Changes the field, auto-dereferencing
Changes a copy of the struct
explanation: Field access through a pointer dereferences automatically: no -> and no (*p).

title: new
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Allocates uninitialized memory
Calls the Buffer constructor function
Allocates a zeroed Buffer, returns a pointer
explanation: new(T) is &T{} for any type: zeroed memory and a pointer; there are no constructors in the language.

title: Embedding
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A parent class User inherits from
An embedded struct, fields promoted
A field named Entity of type Entity
explanation: Embedding a type without a field name promotes its fields and methods, so u.ID works; it is composition, not inheritance.

title: Value receiver
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A method on User that works on a copy
A static function
A method that can modify the caller's User
explanation: A value receiver gets a copy; changes to u inside do not reach the caller, like taking self by value.

title: Pointer receiver
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A method on a copy
A method on the User type itself
A method that modifies the caller's User
explanation: A pointer receiver sees the caller's value, like &mut self; Go takes the address automatically when calling it on a variable.

title: Calling a pointer method
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Does not compile without (&u).Rename
Calls the pointer method on &u automatically
Calls it on a copy, u stays "a"
explanation: Go inserts the & for addressable variables, so u.Rename("b") renames u.

title: Struct comparison
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Compares addresses
Does not compile without an Eq implementation
Compares field by field
explanation: Structs whose fields are all comparable support == out of the box; no derive(PartialEq).

title: Struct tags
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: The field's default value
A comment attached to the field
Metadata encoding/json reads for the name
explanation: Tags are strings attached to fields and read via reflection, the way serde attributes name fields.

title: Interface type
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A set of methods a type must have
An abstract base class
A struct with one function field
explanation: An interface is just a method set, like a trait with only required methods and no associated types.

title: Implicit implementation
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Valid: having a String method is enough
Does not compile: User never declares Stringer
Converts User to a string and stores it in s
explanation: Interfaces are implemented implicitly: having the methods is all it takes, there is no impl Trait for.

title: Interface parameter
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A generic type parameter
A pointer to a Notifier struct
Any value with a Notify method
explanation: An interface parameter is dynamic dispatch, like &dyn Trait; the concrete type is chosen at the call site.

title: any
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An untyped variable
A null-able value
A value of any type
explanation: any is an alias for interface{}, the empty interface every type satisfies; it is Go's Box<dyn Any>.

title: Type assertion
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Casts v to User, truncating it
Calls the function User with v
Checks v holds a User and extracts it
explanation: x.(T) asks an interface value for its concrete type; the two-result form reports success instead of panicking.

title: Type switch
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Branches on the concrete type held by v
Converts v to each type in turn
Switches on the type name as a string
explanation: A type switch is a match over dynamic types; in each case x has that case's type.

title: Embedded interface
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Two fields
The union of both method sets
Two implementations to choose from
explanation: An interface may embed others, combining their methods, like trait A: B + C.

title: nil interface
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Always false for interfaces
True when the held value is zero
True when the interface holds no value
explanation: An interface value is nil only when it holds no concrete value at all; the zero value of any interface is nil.

title: The error type
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An interface: anything with Error() string
A struct holding an error message string
A base class every exception extends
explanation: error is an ordinary interface; any type with an Error() string method is an error, and the stdlib defines it exactly like this.

title: Error check
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Panics and exits the program
Returns the error to the caller
Logs the error and keeps going
explanation: This is what Rust's ? expands to; Go has no ?, so these three lines are written out every time.

title: errors.New
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Throws an exception with that message
Logs the message as an error
Creates an error value with that message
explanation: Errors are plain values; a package-level one like ErrNotFound is a sentinel callers can compare against.

title: Wrapping with %w
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Wraps err so the chain can be inspected
Prints err as plain text into the message
Writes err to the file at path
explanation: %w keeps the original error inside the new one; %v would flatten it to text and break errors.Is and errors.As.

title: errors.Is
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: True if ErrNotFound is anywhere in err's chain
True only if err is exactly ErrNotFound
Compares the two messages
explanation: errors.Is unwraps through %w layers to find a sentinel, where == would miss a wrapped one.

title: errors.As
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Finds a *NotFoundError in the chain
Converts err to a NotFoundError
Compares err with nf for equality
explanation: errors.As is the typed match through the chain, like downcasting with a pointer to fill.

title: Custom error type
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Makes *NotFoundError an error
Overrides the default error message
Declares a method that errors can call
explanation: Implementing Error() string is all a type needs to be an error; no impl std::error::Error ceremony.

title: goroutine
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Runs worker concurrently without waiting
Declares a function named worker
Calls worker and waits for it to return
explanation: The go keyword starts a goroutine, like thread::spawn but cheap; it returns no handle, so waiting is done with channels or a WaitGroup.

title: goroutine with a closure
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Starts a goroutine running the closure
Defines a function to run later
Runs the closure synchronously
explanation: go func(){...}() launches an inline closure; since Go 1.22 each loop iteration has its own i, so the capture is safe.

title: Unbuffered channel
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A channel where send waits for a receiver
An unbounded queue of ints
A channel that holds exactly one value
explanation: An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous: both sides block until the other arrives, unlike an mpsc channel that queues.

title: Buffered channel
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A channel that queues up to 10 values
A channel of 10-element arrays
A channel for exactly 10 goroutines
explanation: The second argument is the buffer size; sends block only when the buffer is full.

title: Send and receive
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Closes the channel
Receives a value, waiting if none is ready
Sends a value, waiting for a receiver
explanation: The arrow shows the data direction: ch <- v sends, <-ch receives.

title: Channel direction
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A receive-only channel
A send-only channel
A channel that is closed
explanation: chan<- T can only be sent to and <-chan T only received from; the compiler enforces the direction at the signature.

title: close and range
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Receives exactly once
Iterates a snapshot of the channel
Receives until the channel is closed
explanation: range over a channel loops until the sender calls close; closing is a signal, not a destruction.

title: select
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Tries each case once, in order
Waits for whichever case is ready first
Runs every case that is ready
explanation: select is a switch over channel operations; it blocks until one case can proceed and picks randomly among ready ones.

title: select with default
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Runs when the channel is closed
Runs at once if no case is ready
Runs after the send succeeds
explanation: A default case makes select non-blocking: it is the try_send pattern.

title: WaitGroup
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Waits for the first task to finish
Cancels the tasks still running
Blocks until every Done matches an Add
explanation: WaitGroup is a counter: Add before starting, Done when finished, Wait to join; it is how you join goroutines, which have no handles.

title: Mutex
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A lock that must be initialized first
A lock protecting n, usable in its zero state
A read-only guard
explanation: The mutex is a field, not a wrapper around the data; its zero value is unlocked and ready, and the compiler does not enforce that n is only touched under it.

title: context
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A structured logger for the call
Carries cancellation and deadlines
The body of the incoming request
explanation: ctx is passed as the first parameter through every layer; ctx.Done() is a channel that closes on cancel, the closest thing to a cancellation token.

title: Generic function
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A two-element array type
Two unconstrained type parameters
Two interface-typed parameters
explanation: Type parameters go in square brackets before the regular parameters; any means unconstrained, like <T, U>.

title: Type inference
highlight: Map(users, func(u User) string { return u.Name })
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Does not compile: T and U must be written
Calls Map with T and U inferred
Calls a method named Map on users
explanation: Type arguments are inferred from the values passed, so callers rarely write Map[User, string].

title: comparable
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: K must implement a Compare method
K must be a number
K must support ==, as map keys must
explanation: comparable is the built-in constraint for types usable with == and as map keys, roughly Eq + Hash.

title: Constraint interface
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Three method names the type must have
A bitwise or of three types
A union of allowed underlying types
explanation: A constraint may list types; ~int admits any type whose underlying type is int, so a defined type like Level still qualifies.

title: Generic type
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A stack whose elements are interfaces
A struct parameterized by an element type
An array of Stack
explanation: Types take parameters too, and methods repeat the parameter list on the receiver, Stack[T]; there are no generic methods beyond that.
